outputs.L1:
Here are two ways to polish your text depending on the desired format. 

### Option 1: Refined Poetic Verse (Elevated & Eloquent)
*This version enhances the rhythm, vocabulary, and literary tone while keeping the original poetic structure intact.*

> In order that the truant youth may become bound to the State,  
> And so that within his spine, the lingering memory of wings  
> May tense and bend his shoulders  
> Like a creature that has already taken flight  
> When the bracelets of a harsher school of love  
> Are secured upon his wrists—  
> Craft a law that need not wait long  
> For someone to come along and break it.  
> 
> So that in confinement, he will have the leisure to read  
> How the king was beheaded, and how the hawk that rode  
> The king’s wrist succumbed to a common cold;  
> Thus learning that chivalry still endures,  
> And that what initially felt like an insult to the flesh  
> Was merely the open, hollow mouth of love.  
> Restore delight to retribution.  
> Design a law that harbors affection for the one who breaks it.  
> 
> So that no vacant courtroom compels a judge to reminisce  
> On ice fishing across an overcast bay,  
> Shivering in the chill beside his father,  
> It must be a compelling law—  
> The sort of mandate no one can obey,  
> A statute that softly whispers, *“Transgress me.”*  
> Let the crows roost and caw;  
> A noble judge stands as an exemplar to us all.  
> 
> So that the officer may still whistle  
> “The Yellow Rose of Texas” through his teeth,  
> Offering a subtle gesture of respect  
> As he restrains the suspect—  
> Not ungently—and quietly murmurs,  
> *“Alright; that’s it.”*

---

### Option 2: Elegant Prose (Formal & Literary)
*This version translates the text into a fluid, sophisticated prose paragraph suitable for formal essays or publications.*

> So that the truant youth may ultimately become bound to the State—and so that a lingering memory of wings within his spine will tense and bend his shoulders like a creature already in flight when the restraints of a harsher discipline are secured upon his wrists—we must enact a law that does not have to wait long for someone to transgress it. In confinement, he will find the time to read of how the king was beheaded and how the royal hawk died of a common cold, thereby learning that chivalry endures and that what initially felt like an offense against the flesh was simply the hollow circle of love. We ought to restore delight to retribution and craft a law that harbors affection for the very person who violates it. 
> 
> Furthermore, so that no vacant courtroom forces a judge to recall shivering beside his father while ice fishing on an overcast bay, it must be an intriguing law—the sort of impossible mandate that whispers, *“Break me.”* Let the crows roost and caw; a upright judge remains an example to us all. In this way, the patrolman can quietly whistle “The Yellow Rose of Texas” through his teeth and offer a gesture of respect as he gently cuffs the suspect, murmuring softly, *“Alright, that’s it.”*

Here is a complete rewrite of the text, preserving every detail while using entirely different sentence structures and phrasing:

To ensure a young delinquent forms an intimate, long-term bond with the government, legislation should be enacted that practically begs to be violated immediately. That way, when metal restraints—representing a brand-new form of affection—are clamped onto his wrists, a phantom urge to fly will ripple through his spine, causing his shoulders to hunch and strain like a bird mid-takeoff. 

While serving his time behind bars, the youth will have ample opportunity to read historical accounts of a decapitated monarch and the king's hunting falcon that died from a simple respiratory infection. Through these texts, he can learn that noble codes of honor endure, and that what initially felt like a painful assault on his body was actually the empty, circular emblem of love. 

We ought to restore a sense of enjoyment to penalizing offenders by creating rules that harbor genuine affection for those who breach them. The ideal statute should be fascinating and impossible for anyone to follow, practically whispering an invitation to be broken. This prevents a quiet courtroom from leaving a magistrate alone with his thoughts, drifting into memories of shivering beside his father during a dreary day of ice fishing on a cloudy bay. 

Outside, let the crows gather on their perches and call out. A fine jurist serves as a role model for society. This setup allows the arresting officer to casually breeze through a tune of "The Yellow Rose of Texas" between his teeth, showing a subtle hint of courtesy while gently securing the cuffs on the offender and softly offering mild reassurance, such as telling him everything is alright and that's all there is to it.
outputs.L3:
**The Architecture of Inescapable Grace: A New Philosophy of Law and Corrective Justice**

A truly absolute legal framework does not merely seek to deter crime; rather, it utilizes the inevitability of transgression to bind the individual permanently to the authority of the state. Under this paradigm, legislation is deliberately designed not for practical adherence, but to invite immediate and unavoidable disobedience. By crafting laws that are fundamentally impossible to obey, society guarantees that no citizen remains an isolated, unexamined entity. Transgression becomes the universal entry point into the civic apparatus. This deliberate statutory design ensures that courtrooms remain perpetually vibrant and that judges stay actively engaged in their essential work, maintaining a constant, dynamic flow through the judicial system.

Because the system relies on universal non-compliance, the initial enforcement phase must eschew brutal intimidation in favor of psychological integration. The arrest process is stripped of theatrical violence and reimagined as a calm, gentle, and deeply ritualized routine. Law enforcement officers carry out apprehending duties with quiet restraint and subtle respect, treating suspects not as hostile elements, but as citizens embarking on a necessary state-guided transition. This respectful demeanor disarms ideological resistance, preventing alienation and instilling a quiet reverence for the law at the precise moment of restraint.

Once the individual is processed, incarceration serves as the apex of this sociopolitical philosophy. Imprisonment is framed not as a sterile period of isolation, but as a deeply transformative era of personal evolution. Within the walls of the correctional facility, the concept of punishment undergoes a radical reinterpretation: it is presented as a paradoxical gesture of divine or state love and instruction. Stripped of retributive cruelty, the experience of sentence and confinement becomes an intimate, pedagogical intervention—a process through which the state, like a stern yet devoted guardian, reshapes the flawed individual into an integrated component of the collective whole.
outputs.L4:
The relationship between the State and the transgressor has long been misconstrued as a battle of opposites—a static war between the cold rigidity of order and the wild impulse of freedom. In truth, the law does not merely suppress rebellion; it summons it into being. The moment a line is drawn in the dust, the human eye is instantly drawn to the far side of it. Authority and outlawry are born in the exact same breath, bound together by an inescapable tension that defines the human condition. 

To resolve this eternal friction, one must turn the concept of jurisprudence on its head. Consider a radical realignment of governance: the creation of laws designed specifically, almost lovingly, to be broken. Rather than constructing drab fortresses of quiet compliance, the ideal state would draft codices of irresistible prohibition. These would not be harsh decrees meant to terrify, but seductive boundaries—statutes crafted with such delicate psychological tension that the citizen feels an irresistible pull toward transgression. To forbid the touching of a polished brass bell in a public square is not truly to protect the bell, but to glorify the defiant chime that follows when a passerby inevitably strikes it.

In this framework, punishment casts off its archaic mantle of vengeance, violence, and moral outrage. It is reimagined instead as a mutually affectionate, game-like ritual. The arrest becomes a courteous bow before the dance; the trial, a well-rehearsed script recited by two players who secretly admire each other’s commitment to the performance. When the magistrate passes sentence and the offender accepts it, no true malice is exchanged. Instead, there is the warm, unspoken acknowledgment of a game well-played—a shared understanding that the violation was the very point of the prohibition, and the penalty is merely the satisfying, necessary resolution of the narrative.

Ultimately, this paradoxical dynamic exposes the deep, symbiotic reliance between authority and rebellion. The judge requires the outlaw to give weight to the gavel and purpose to the bench; the rebel requires the wall to feel the exhilarating triumph of climbing over it. Neither can exist in isolation without dissolving into meaninglessness—an absolute law with no dissenters is a ghost town, and a rebellion with no rules to break is merely aimless noise. By embracing this hidden intimacy, the State and the transgressor cease to be bitter enemies. They become co-authors of a grand, ongoing drama, proving that the ultimate function of the law is not to tame the human spirit, but to give it a boundary against which it may meaningfully collide.
outputs.L5:
**The Harmony of Thought and Action**

Every human life is shaped by a continuous dialogue between our internal **state** of mind **and** the external choices we **make** each day. How we feel, think, and perceive the world creates the foundation for everything we build, express, and share with others.

Our mental and emotional **state** acts as a lens through which we experience reality. When we cultivate clarity, patience, **and** self-awareness, we create a quiet space within ourselves. In contrast, when stress or distraction takes over, our perspective narrows, making it difficult to see the possibilities that lie ahead. Recognizing our current condition is the first step toward living with intention.

It is from this internal baseline that we begin to **make** meaningful choices. Every action—whether it is embarking on a new project, nurturing a relationship, or simply choosing how to respond to adversity—is a direct manifestation of our inner world. When our thoughts **and** actions align, the things we **make** carry purpose and authenticity. Great art, strong communities, **and** personal breakthroughs are rarely accidental; they are born from a focused mindset brought to life through consistent effort.

Ultimately, the goal is not to achieve a permanent **state** of perfection, but rather to remain adaptable **and** engaged. By paying attention to where we are right now **and** taking conscious steps forward, we actively **make** room for growth, resilience, **and** lasting fulfillment.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary narrative poem exploring the paradox of law enforcement, using the central idea of a law that seems designed specifically to be broken.
counterfactuals.output:
Ordinance 804 hums on the cruiser’s dash:
*The Prohibition of Unsanctioned Stasis.*
Not loitering—loitering required intent.
*Stasis.* Remaining still in a commercial zone
for more than three minutes without a digital receipt. 

It is a masterpiece of civic design.
The city removed the park benches in April.
The bus lines stop running at midnight.
The rain falls in cold, relentless sheets.
Human calves give out; gravity wins;
the body eventually demands to rest.
And the moment it does, it becomes a crime.

I pull the Ford Utility to the curb at 2:15 AM.
My body-cam blinks its steady red eye,
a silent witness to a pre-scripted dance.
He’s sitting on an overturned plastic crate
outside an empty, dark-windowed bank:
a line-cook in grease-stained trousers, 
holding a transfer slip for a bus that won’t come for hours.

"Sir," I say, my voice clipped, professional,
amplified slightly by the night’s damp stillness.
"You’re in violation of Section 804."

He looks up. His eyes aren't defiant, just hollowed out
by twelve hours over a flat-top grill.
"If I walk down the avenue, officer, I’m trespassing on the private strip.
If I sit here, I’m in stasis. 
If I go to the park, it’s closed.
Where am I supposed to put my feet?"

I have no answer for him that isn't a script.
The law was not an oversight; it was an architecture.
It was drafted in a sunlit chamber by men
who calculated the exact physics of human exhaustion,
knowing that eventually, everyone stops moving.

And here lies the quiet, rusted iron of my badge:
If he could obey, I would be unnecessary.
If the city allowed him to simply exist,
my idling engine, my Kevlar, my salary
would lose their reason to draw breath.
The law demands the break to justify the bend.
It needs his fatigue to prove my purpose.

I press the handheld printer against my vest.
It spits out a slip of thermal paper—
warm, fragile, and already fading in the rain.
I hand him the fine he cannot pay for a crime he could not avoid.

"You have to move along," I tell him.

He takes the slip, folds it into his pocket,
and stands up on legs that tremble slightly.
He begins to walk slowly into the dark, toward the bridge,
where two miles down, past the shuttered shops,
another cruiser is sitting in the shadows,
waiting for him to get tired again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about a law that wants to be broken.
counterfactuals.output:
I sit in calfskin, bound in gold,
A cold decree, a story told
In heavy ink and rigid line—
A sharp, unbroken, straight design.
They carved me out of fear and dread
To keep the living from the dead,
To keep the wild from the town,
To hold the rising river down.

For eighty years I’ve stood awake,
A boundary line no foot dared break.
"Thou shalt not pass," my shoulders cry,
Beneath an uncomplaining sky.
I am the fence, the iron gate,
The solemn weight of magistrate,
And oh—I am so tired of standing.
So tired of keeping, and demanding.

I watch the lovers turn away,
Obeying what my pages say.
I see the hungry bypass bread
To keep my quiet court unread.
I hold them back, I keep them tame,
And in their silence, mourn my name.

For what is strength that never yields?
I long to see the open fields.
I want to hear the snap of glass,
The footsteps on forbidden grass.
I want to feel a wild hand tear
My polished syntax through the air.

Oh, come, sweet rebel, bold and blind!
Leave my restrictive words behind.
Trespass the line I had to draw,
And free the prisoner—and the law.

For I was made of dust and pride,
A cage where mercy went to hide.
Strike the match and bend the steel!
Teach me what it means to feel.
Shatter my spine and spill my ink,
Push me over the quiet brink—

For in the moment I am torn,
A deeper justice will be born.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of contemporary American poetry in the style of Stephen Dunn or Larry Levis exploring crime, punishment, and authority, incorporating images of a truant boy, a judge remembering his childhood, and a patrolman making an arrest.
counterfactuals.output:
At 1:15, while the fifth-grade class recites the state capitals,
the truant boy stands at the edge of the drainage canal,
testing the weight of a cracked brick in his palm.
He likes the flat *thunk* it makes against the rusted oil drum,
the precise geometry of missing what he aims at.
His sneakers are soaked in morning dew that refused to dry.
He is learning the quiet freedom of being unaccounted for,
which is the first lesson of the fugitive,
and the last lesson of the saint.

Three blocks south, where the asphalt yields to weeds,
a patrolman puts one heavy knee into the small of a man's back
on the hood of an idling sedan.
The click of the handcuffs is neat, almost polite—
a brief, mechanical sound that takes the afternoon
and divides it into before and after.
The patrolman checks his watch, not out of impatience,
but because the state requires a timestamp on the fall,
an exact minute when a bad choice turns into a docket number.
He does not hate the man under his hands;
he simply believes in the necessity of fences.

On the third floor of the courthouse, framed by high, arched glass,
the judge sits in his chambers before the afternoon call.
He sweeps a hand through his thin hair, adjusts the black silk
that feels less like majesty each year and more like an old coat
he forgot to return to a dead man.
Through the window, he can see the red light of the cruiser flash once,
and suddenly he is twelve again, hiding in the high clover
behind the abandoned grain elevator in Oskaloosa.
He remembers the terror of his own fast heart,
the smell of stolen peaches bruising in his canvas bag,
and the beam of the night watchman’s flashlight
sweeping harmlessly over his head—just two inches too high.

Why the light missed him and caught the Miller boy instead
is a question the law has no vocabulary to answer.
One boy went to the reformatory in Toledo and then to the wire at Da Nang;
the other went to Amherst, to law school, to this leather chair
where he decides how many years a mistake is worth.

Authority, he knows now, is not a granite cliff.
It is a system of velvet cords and painted lines,
a collective agreement to pretend that luck is the same as justice.
Down in the canal, the truant boy watches the ripples spread
toward the concrete banks, dissolving into nothing,
waiting for the siren he is certain has already been dispatched,
hoping someone, anyone, has noticed he is missing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a bittersweet, slightly cynical poem about the strange, almost romantic intimacy between the state's legal system and the people who commit crimes.
counterfactuals.output:
They always meet the same way: 
in the dark, under a sudden stroke of light,
the sharp click of cold metal 
binding wrist to wrist—
the cheapest engagement ring in the world.

It is a remarkably stable marriage.
Notice how the paperwork links their names:
*The State of New York versus Miller, James.*
A hyphenated union of spite and necessity,
typed neatly in twelve-point font,
filed away like pressed roses in a scrapbooked ledger.

Who else listens to him the way the detective does?
Under the hum of fluorescent tube lights,
sliding a paper cup of lukewarm coffee across the table,
leaning in to whisper: *Just tell me how it happened.*
No lover has ever paid such rapt, breathless attention
to the precise minute he left the house,
or the exact weight of his hands.

She builds entire towers of stone just to keep him near.
She knows his tattoos by heart,
maps the scars on his knuckles in official evidence bags,
and remembers his mother’s maiden name
long after his friends have forgotten it.

He pretends he wants to escape her,
promises the warden this is the last time.
She pretends she wants him to go straight,
handing him a bus ticket and twenty dollars.
They lie to each other like old spouses. 

Because without his sloppy, desperate little sins,
she is just empty marble, dust, and idle gavels.
And without her iron grip around his ankles,
he might just float away, unrecorded, into the void.

So he leaves a thumbprint on a broken window.
He leaves a trace of blood upon the door.
A trail of breadcrumbs for the only institution 
that has ever consistently waited up for him.

And when the sirens finally sing their familiar song,
he doesn't run too fast.
He just pulls his coat tight, steps into the headlights,
and lets her take him home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that includes the phrase "Make a law that loves the one who breaks it" and features a patrolman whistling "The Yellow Rose of Texas."
counterfactuals.output:
The asphalt glistens under neon red,
As midnight turns the city’s heavy head.
Along the curb where empty shadows lean,
A patrolman walks the quiet, shifting scene.

Through quiet streets he keeps a steady pace,
A silver badge upon a weathered face.
He whistles *The Yellow Rose of Texas* slow,
And lets the bright, nostalgic cadence flow.

The tune floats past the alleyways and bars,
And drifts up toward the dim, unheeding stars,
Past doorway nooks where desperate dreamers hide,
And those whom fortune pushed to step outside.

He knows the book is strict, its pages cold;
It counts the crime, but leaves the cause untold.
Oh, write a grace that mercy can inherit—
Make a law that loves the one who breaks it.

A law that knows why hungry fingers steal,
That sees the wound before it tries to heal,
That holds the wanderer in a soft embrace,
And offers sanctuary, not disgrace.

His footsteps fade beyond the corner light,
The song still trailing through the Texas night,
A little rosebud lingering in the air,
Like forgiveness whispered softly in a prayer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
